title: Five Ways to Cook Dehydrated Kiri Kos
excerpt: Kiri Kos is mature Sri Lankan jackfruit, dehydrated for the pantry. Here are five easy ways to cook it at home, wherever you live.
content:
## What is Kiri Kos?

Kiri Kos is Leora Naturale's dehydrated jackfruit: mature Sri Lankan kos, cut and dried in dehydration machines so it keeps in the cupboard for months. It is 100% jackfruit with no preservatives, packed in a clear 50 g pouch. Soak it, and it cooks like fresh kos.

## First, rehydrate it

1. Put the pieces in a bowl and cover with lukewarm water.
2. Soak for 45 to 60 minutes, until soft.
3. Drain well, then cook.

## 1. Kiri kos curry

The classic. Simmer the soaked kos with coconut milk, curry leaves, garlic, turmeric and roasted curry powder until creamy. Serve with rice and a sambol, the way it is made at home.

## 2. Kos mallum

Chop the soaked kos finely and toss it in a hot pan with grated coconut, green chilli, red onion and a squeeze of lime. A quick, fresh side dish.

## 3. Tempered kos

Fry onion, dried chilli, mustard seeds and curry leaves in a little oil, add the drained kos and a pinch of chilli flakes, and stir-fry until the edges brown.

## 4. Kos cutlets

Mash cooked kos with boiled potato, onion, green chilli and pepper. Roll into balls, crumb them and fry for a party snack that tastes of home.

## 5. Keep a pouch in the pantry abroad

Fresh jackfruit is hard to find in Australia, Canada, the Middle East or Russia. A light pouch of Kiri Kos needs no refrigeration, so you can cook kos curry any weekend, or send a pouch to family overseas.

title: Butterfly Pea Flower: Blue Tea and Blue String Hoppers
excerpt: Nil katarolu turns water a vivid blue. Here is how to brew butterfly pea flower tea and use it to colour string hoppers, rice and desserts naturally.
content:
## What is butterfly pea flower?

Butterfly pea (Clitoria ternatea) is a climbing vine with deep blue flowers. In Sinhala it is නිල් කටරොළු (nil katarolu) and in Tamil சங்குப்பூ (sangu poo). Dried, the flowers brew into a caffeine-free drink with a vivid, natural blue colour. Leora Naturale packs 100% dried butterfly pea flowers in Sri Lanka, 10 g per pouch.

## How do you make butterfly pea flower tea?

1. Put a few dried flowers in a cup.
2. Pour over warm water.
3. Steep for 3 to 5 minutes, until the water turns deep blue.
4. Strain and enjoy it plain, or with honey.

## Why does it turn purple with lime?

The blue colour reacts to acid. Squeeze in a little lime and the cup turns violet in seconds, which children love to watch.

## How do you make blue string hoppers?

Brew a strong cup of butterfly pea tea and let it cool. Use it instead of plain water when you mix your idiyappam flour, then press and steam the string hoppers as usual. They come out a soft natural blue with no artificial colour.

## What else can I colour with it?

- Rice: add the brew to the cooking water for blue rice.
- Desserts: colour puddings, jelly and icing.
- Drinks: make blue lemonade, then watch it change with lime.

## How should I store it?

Keep the pouch sealed in a cool, dry place so the flowers stay crisp and the colour stays bright.

title: How to Make Masala Chai with Sri Lankan Spices
excerpt: A cup of masala tea made with Sri Lankan cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, ginger, nutmeg, fennel and pepper, using Leora Naturale Chai Masala.
content:
## What is chai masala?

Chai masala is a ground spice blend for masala tea. Leora Naturale Chai Masala uses seven Sri Lankan spices: cinnamon (kurundu), cardamom (karadamungu), cloves (karabu neti), ginger (inguru), nutmeg (sadikka), fennel (maduru) and black pepper (gammiris). It is a muddy brown powder with no tea leaves, so you add it to your own tea.

## How do you make masala chai?

1. Bring one cup of water to the boil with one teaspoon of black tea or one tea bag.
2. Add a small pinch of Chai Masala.
3. Pour in half a cup of milk and simmer for two to three minutes.
4. Sweeten with sugar or jaggery, strain and serve hot.

Use more spice for a stronger cup, less for a gentle one.

## Why Sri Lankan spices?

Sri Lanka is famous for true cinnamon, and its cardamom, cloves, nutmeg and pepper are grown on the same island. That is the flavour of a Sri Lankan kitchen in every cup.

## Other ways to use it

- Stir a pinch into hot milk before bed.
- Add it to cake, cookie or pancake batter.
- Sprinkle it over porridge.

## How should I store it?

Keep the pouch sealed in a cool, dry place away from sunlight so the spices keep their aroma.

title: What Is Heen Bovitiya Tea and How Do You Brew It?
excerpt: Heen Bovitiya is a traditional Sri Lankan herbal tea. Here is what it is, how to brew a cup at home, and where to buy it abroad from Leora Naturale.
content:
## What is Heen Bovitiya tea?

Heen Bovitiya tea is a traditional Sri Lankan herbal tea made from the leaves of Osbeckia octandra, a flowering shrub that grows across the island. It is caffeine-free and is not related to black or green tea. Leora Naturale packs it in Sri Lanka in boxes of 25 or 15 tea bags and ships it to Sri Lankan families abroad.

## Where does it come from?

Heen Bovitiya grows wild in Sri Lanka and has been brewed in village kitchens for generations. For many families it was the cup that was always on the stove: simple, earthy and tied to memories of home. That is why so many Sri Lankans overseas go looking for it.

## How do you brew Heen Bovitiya tea?

Each Leora Naturale pack holds 25 or 15 tea bags, so brewing takes no measuring.

1. Bring fresh water to the boil.
2. Put one tea bag in a cup.
3. Pour the hot water over the bag.
4. Steep for five to seven minutes. Leave it longer for a stronger cup.
5. Remove the bag and enjoy it warm.

If the brewing guide printed on your pack differs, follow the pack.

## How does it taste?

Expect a light, floral, slightly earthy flavour. Many people drink it plain. Others add a little honey, jaggery or a squeeze of lime, the way it is often served at home.

## What goes well with it?

Heen Bovitiya is a quiet evening cup. On other days, try its sister products: Heen Bovitiya powder stirred into warm water, or a bright blue cup of butterfly pea flower tea.

## Is it easy to keep and ship abroad?

Yes. The herb is dried, so the tea is light, compact and needs no refrigeration. Keep the pouch sealed in a cool, dry place and it travels well to Australia, Canada, the Middle East and Russia.

content:
## Can you buy Sri Lankan food abroad?

Yes. Many Sri Lankans in Australia, Canada, the Middle East and Russia now order foods from home online, and dehydrated products are among the easiest to send because they stay fresh and light on long journeys. Leora Naturale makes Kiri Kos (dehydrated jackfruit), Heen Bovitiya tea and powder, Butterfly Pea Flower and Chai Masala in Sri Lanka and ships them abroad.

## How does dehydration work?

Dehydration gently removes most of the water from fruit, vegetables or leaves. Without water there is far less for spoilage to grow on, so the food keeps much longer. Leora Naturale uses dehydration machines at controlled, low temperatures, not the sun, so every batch dries evenly and cleanly. The flavour stays concentrated, which is why dehydrated jackfruit tastes so familiar.

## Why is dehydrated food good for shipping?

- It is light. Removing water keeps shipping costs down.
- It is compact. Pouches pack flat and take little space.
- It needs no refrigeration. Parcels can travel for days or weeks without a cold chain.
- It lasts. A sealed pouch kept cool and dry stays good for months.

title: The Art of Natural Dehydration
excerpt: How low-temperature dehydration keeps Sri Lankan fruit and vegetables shelf-stable without chemical preservatives.
content:
Leora Naturale preserves food by taking water out slowly. That is the whole method. Low-temperature dehydration is not frying, not freeze-drying, and not a chemical soak. Moisture leaves the fruit or vegetable so microbes cannot grow, while colour, aroma, and most of the nutrient load stay in the flesh.

High heat scorches natural sugars and fades greens. A gentle, controlled temperature avoids that. Kiri Kos (mature jackfruit) comes out kitchen-ready: rehydrate it in lukewarm water for 45–60 minutes, then cook as you would the fresh harvest. Herbs and flowers such as Heen Bovitiya and butterfly pea keep their colour and aroma for the cup.

Because water is the only thing removed, the pack does not need artificial preservatives. Sealed and kept cool and dry, a Leora Naturale pack keeps for 6 months to 1 year, depending on the product. The best-before date is printed on every pack.

Every batch starts with named Sri Lankan produce. Jackfruit is Artocarpus heterophyllus. Heen Bovitiya is Osbeckia octandra. Butterfly pea is Clitoria ternatea. Using the botanical name as well as the kitchen name (kos, nil katarolu) helps cooks and search engines know exactly what is in the pack.

title: Why Preservative-Free Food Matters
excerpt: A practical guide to choosing dehydrated Sri Lankan snacks and cooking vegetables that stay good without chemicals.
content:
Most shelf-stable snacks stay edible because something extra was added: sugar, oil, salt, or a listed preservative. Dehydration takes a different path. Remove the water and the same fruit or vegetable keeps without those extras.

That is the Leora Naturale rule. Kiri Kos is 100% jackfruit. Heen Bovitiya tea and powder are 100% herb, Butterfly Pea Flower is 100% flower, and Chai Masala is only spices. Labels state 100% natural, product of Sri Lanka.

For a weekday curry when the market has no fresh kos, soak a pack of Kiri Kos and cook. Diaspora kitchens use the same method when the island vegetable is out of season or thousands of kilometres away.

Preservative-free is not a slogan here. It is the process: low-temperature drying, careful packing, a sealed shelf life of 6 months to 1 year, depending on the product.
